/Through Sunday/...
Issued at 1122 PM MST Sun Nov 1 2026

The next storm system has started to affect our area over the last 
few hours with some light rain/snow showers across the high country 
and light rain showers for the majority of the plains. Some light 
rain/snow showers continue at this hour for the Medicine Bow Range 
and light rain showers for the far northeastern plains. With the 
saturated grounds from the Sunday evening rain, fog is possible once 
again. Favored locations look to be northern Colorado and possibly 
extending into the northern metro and east to DIA. Have held off on 
any highlights given the uncertainty with how widespread any fog 
would be, but an advisory may be needed if confidence increases 
overnight. Any fog would quickly lift as the cold front moves 
through on Monday morning.

The trough that will affect our weather over the next 24-36 hours is 
currently centered over the Great Basin and should quickly push 
through Colorado by late Monday. Good moisture continues to advect 
into our area with southwest flow in the mid and upper levels. We 
expect coverage of precipitation to increase by Monday morning 
through the early afternoon as lift increases and the cold front 
pushes through from north to south. The cold front moves through the 
metro around 6-9am and looks to clear our area by about 2pm Monday. 
In its wake, afternoon temperatures should struggle to make it out 
of the upper 40s for much of the plains given the clouds in place 
and the chance for showers. Some scattered showers could linger on 
the plains through Tuesday morning with some upslope continuing.

QPF is very similar to the last forecast package. Ensemble guidance 
continues to coalesce on 0.1-0.4" rainfall for the Denver metro with 
some locally higher amounts possible mainly for the southeast 
portions of the metro. Similar rainfall totals look possible for 
most of the plains with some signal that western Washington County 
and adjacent areas could see the most rainfall. This is likely due 
to a rather deep upslope component (northerly winds) from the 
surface up to 500 mb behind the cold front. For the northern high 
country, many areas should see 0.50-0.75" QPF with some higher 
amounts possible. Lesser amounts are expected for the rest of the 
high country.

As for snow, snow showers will start to increase in coverage over 
the next few hours for the high country. Colder air will continue to 
filter in aloft quickly lowering snow levels. Snow levels are 
currently around 10,500 feet, but quickly drop through the overnight 
to around 9,250 feet by Monday morning. Snow levels will continue to 
drop to near 7,500-8,000 feet or even a bit lower by Monday evening. 
The Palmer Divide still has a chance for some snowflakes to mix in 
on Monday evening as precipitation chances start to wind down. The 
Winter Weather Advisory goes into effect early this morning and 
lasts through late Monday night. The forecast remains on track with 
3-8 inches of snowfall expected in general. As previously noted, 
northerly flow is expected as the trough pushes through. In this 
flow pattern, the northern mountains continue to look most favored 
in our area for the highest snowfall totals with some totals greater 
than 9 inches possible, particularly at the highest elevations. DESI 
probabilities highlight this potential well with a 50% chance or 
greater of snowfall totals exceeding 6 inches for the Park Range, 
northern Gore Range, and Medicine Bow Range. Note that higher totals 
are still possible for areas along the Front Range Mountains 
including Summit County and RMNP, but much less likely.

Monday and even Tuesday will also feature some breezy conditions for 
the plains. DESI probabilities show at least a 40% chance for wind 
gusts exceeding 55 mph on Monday afternoon and evening across our 
plains. Given the lack of subsidence and momentum transfer, we have 
held off on any wind highlights. Most locations on the plains should 
see gusts of 35-55 mph with isolated locations having the potential 
for gusts of 55-60 mph Monday afternoon, evening, and into early 
Tuesday. Wind gusts could still reach 40-50 mph for the far eastern 
plains on Tuesday afternoon.

After the passage of the trough late Monday into early Tuesday, 
ridging quickly looks to take its place. Tuesday will be a warmer 
day with high temperatures near average for this time of year- in 
the upper 50s. High temperatures should stay near average for the 
rest of the week. Another low looks to track through our area on 
Wednesday. The majority of models bring the chance for another round 
of light snow showers for the high country and possibly some rain 
showers for the plains. Any accumulation continues to look rather 
unimpressive with this system at this time. Thursday and Friday 
should be dry with westerly flow aloft and near-normal temperatures.

By the weekend, there could be another cold front cooling 
temperatures down as hinted in the EC
